Patel will also highlight internal bureau reforms that shifted more than 1,000 agents and staff into field operations, along with the opening of a new field office in Billings, Montana, as part of the FBI's expansion in Indian Country through Operation Steadfast Promise.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Trump’s law-and-order blitz marks one year with eye-popping haul of suspects, guns in blue city
summary: The Memphis Safe Task Force marks its first anniversary with over 12,000 arrests and a 36% drop in crime since Trump deployed the national guard.
story: Retired Chicago Police Chief of Detectives Eugene Roy tells Fox News Digital the city should look to Memphis, where homicides fell sharply after the National Guard moved in, and says local leaders are refusing federal help amid a deepening officer shortage.

FIRST ON FOX: The Memphis Safe Task Force has made more than 12,000 arrests and seized more than 2,100 illegal firearms in its first year, Fox News Digital learned exclusively, as the Trump administration points to the operation's enforcement record amid a drop in crime across the city.

"President Trump’s Memphis Safe Task Force has driven down violent crime in a city that was failed by extreme Democrats’ soft-on-crime policies. The Task Force has made more than 12,000 arrests, including of murderers, sex offenders, drug traffickers and other violent criminals, and has seized more than 2,100 illegal firearms. President Trump restored law and order and made Memphis safe again," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

The task force, launched one year ago Tuesday, brought federal, state and local law enforcement agencies together after President Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum directing the deployment of National Guard personnel to Memphis. The intervention came as Memphis, a Democratic-leaning city in solidly Republican Tennessee, confronted one of the nation’s most severe violent-crime problems, with FBI data showing the city had the highest violent-crime rate in the country in 2024.
BLUE CITY'S STAGGERING 40% VIOLENT CRIME DROP A 'BLUEPRINT FOR OTHER CITIES,' LAW ENFORCEMENT EXPERT SAYS

President Donald Trump signs a Presidential Memorandum that will deploy the National Guard to Memphis, Tennessee, to establish the "Memphis Safe Task Force," Monday, September 15, 2025, in the Oval Office. (Official White House Photo by Molly Riley)

The operation has led to a 36% decrease in overall crime year over year, with motor vehicle thefts down 57%, robberies down 43%, murders down 44% and aggravated assaults down 27%, Fox News Digital learned.
In 2025, overall crime in Memphis was down 28% compared to 2024, data reviewed by Fox News Digital showed.

Memphis resident Darian Glover was convicted in August of distributing fentanyl that caused three fatal overdoses. One victim believed he was buying cocaine, but the substance tested positive for fentanyl.
TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS

Members of the National Guard patrol on October 11, 2025, in Memphis, Tennessee. National Guard members began patrolling Memphis this week as part of a federal task force established by President Trump to combat what the administration says is violent crime in the city. (Photo by Brett Carlsen/Getty Images)
Burglaries are down 27% while shoplifting is down 44%, according to crime data.

In September, the DOJ also sentenced Memphis resident Courtney Trenell to 15 years in prison for serving as a getaway driver in two bank robberies and joining a conspiracy to rob six Memphis-area banks.
Federal law enforcement officers stand at the intersection of Beale St. and N. Second St., Wednesday, Oct. 8, 2025, in Memphis, Tenn. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Memphis was grappling with a severe violent-crime crisis in the years before the task force launched, with homicides surging to 397 in 2023 from 301 a year earlier, according to the Justice Department. From coast to coast, violent crime surged in 2020 and remained elevated in the years immediately afterward, as the nation grappled with coronavirus lockdowns that year and widespread protests and riots.

The Memphis operation is part of a broader Trump administration effort to deploy federal law enforcement resources to cities facing high levels of violent crime. The administration has also launched a federal law-enforcement surge in Washington, D.C., where officials say the effort has produced a sharp decline in crime.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Smithsonian’s dark take on America exposed: Washington dubbed ‘town destroyer,’ Revolutionary War ‘dangerous'
summary: The Smithsonian Institution's American Indians museum labels George Washington a "town destroyer" while omitting key context about the attacks.
story: Reps. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, and Bryan Steil, R-Wis., dissect the Smithsonian's alleged 'woke' agenda, addressing concerns about the museum promoting 'cultural Marxism.' The discussion highlights the importance of objective history and questions taxpayer funding for a museum of anti-American horrors, calling for a change in leadership.

NEW YORK — A Smithsonian museum in Manhattan presents a sharply critical account of George Washington, the Revolutionary War and America’s early years, while some historical context that complicates that narrative is omitted or given less prominent treatment, Fox News Digital found.

The findings come as the Smithsonian faces heightened scrutiny from the Trump administration over how it presents American history. President Donald Trump has ordered a review of the institution’s exhibits and educational materials as part of an effort to change what his administration says is an overly negative portrayal of the country’s history.

Fox News Digital visited the Manhattan branch of the National Museum of the American Indian earlier in September and found exhibits that emphasize the destruction suffered by Native communities while offering comparatively little context about the conflicts and events surrounding American military campaigns.

One display near the center of the museum’s "Native New York" exhibit features an illustration of Washington’s profile — similar to the one that appears on quarters — over a label that reads "town destroyer."
TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER
A display at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York City. (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

The description underneath the image recounts how "American armies destroyed 40 Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) towns and burned their harvests while residents fled," noting that "the Haudenosaunee still call George Washington and all U.S. presidents Hanadahguyus. The name means ‘town destroyer.’"
The panel does not mention the raids on American settlements that led to the campaign or explain why Washington ordered the attack.

"The American destruction of the Six Nations' homelands came as a result of the destructive raids carried out by the Indians and American loyalists on the frontiers of New York and Pennsylvania in 1778," an excerpt from the National Park Service reads. "The raids crippled the American Continental Army by depriving it of food and manpower and spread terror by destroying frontier settlements and taking prisoners."

The exhibit comes as the Trump administration continues its broader dispute with the Smithsonian over how the institution presents American history. Specifically, the president has taken issue with the institution allegedly seeking to divert the telling of American history "away from America’s Founding and the Founders and towards a narrative of a deeply flawed creation of the country."
SMITHSONIAN SHOWDOWN INTENSIFIES AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ISSUES A STARK NEW WARNING
A text box at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York City. (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

The administration has threatened changes to Smithsonian funding and federal-agency support as it presses the institution to alter what it describes as divisive or historically inaccurate portrayals of the country.
Many of the other exhibits in the museum take a similar line to the display on Washington, highlighting the alleged brutality of American settlers while downplaying the violence of natives.

One placard, recounting the history of the Iroquois between 1779 and 1804 from the point of view of a native woman, states that "it was peaceful, she said, until the white men began their revolution."
For roughly 100 years, between 1609 and 1701, the Iroquois were engaged in a series of conflicts with other native tribes over access to animal pelts.
Even before the Trump administration’s current dispute with the Smithsonian, the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C., attracted criticism over how it presents American history.

"​​In recent years, I have been chronicling the evolution of the ‘identity museum’ … designed to affirm a particular group’s claims, outline its accomplishments, boost its pride," a cultural critic wrote for the New York Times in 2010. "The National Museum of the American Indian in Washington — a pioneering example of the genre — jettisons Western scholarship and tells its own story, leading one tribe to solemnly describe its earliest historical milestone: ‘Birds teach people to call for rain.’"
LEGAL EXPERT CALLS FOR SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP OVERHAUL OVER ‘SELF-LOATHING’ PORTRAYAL OF HISTORY: ‘IT’S BILE’
The front entrance of the National Museum of the American Indian in New York City. (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

"Through a gauze of romance, that museum portrays an impossibly peace-loving, harmonious, homogeneous, pastoral world that preceded the invasion of white people — a vision with far less detail and insight than the old natural history museums once provided," the critic continued.
The exhibits acknowledge some conflicts involving Native tribes but focus far more heavily on the violence inflicted on them than on the events that led to the fighting.
The museum also maintains a catalog of online materials geared towards middle school students that generally take the same editorial line.

Teachers, for instance, are instructed to show a video to students that opens by saying that "the American War for independence was such a disruptive and dangerous project." It goes on to frame the actions of American colonists negatively, referring to them as trespassers and squatters.
WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING
President Donald Trump has ordered a review of the Smithsonian's content, ahead of the 250th birthday of the United States' founding. (Getty)
In several displays dealing with the Revolutionary War, the exhibit portrays American actions toward Native allies in sharply negative terms.

A video display near the beginning of the exhibit claims, unequivocally, that an American soldier shot and killed Chief White Eyes, a Lenape chief who had allied with the Americans. The cause of White Eyes’ death, however, is historically contested — something the museum outlines in relatively small text underneath the video display, which states that White Eyes was "probably" murdered by an American soldier.

The museum is housed within the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House, a building formerly used for collecting trade duties and named after the Founding Father to commemorate his role as the first secretary of the Treasury.
HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE'
A bookshelf in the gift shop of the National Museum of the American Indian in New York City. (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

Just before exiting the building, visitors pass a museum store where several books present sharply critical accounts of American history. "An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States," for instance, is displayed prominently on the store shelves.

Among other things, the book criticizes Americans for having a "cult-like" dedication to the Constitution, suggests that the United States was founded upon White supremacy and genocide and claims that the federal government is still carrying out ethnic cleansing against natives. A graphic novel adaptation of the text marketed toward younger readers was also available.

Other titles on display included "Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in US History," "An Afro-Indigenous History of the United States," a tome about the "two spirit" gender identity and a children’s picture book about Deb Haaland, President Joe Biden’s interior secretary.

title: Alito, Thomas shred 'Hail Mary' challenge to federal ballot mail rules in dissent
summary: Justice Samuel Alito called the Supreme Court's refusal to lift a universal injunction against Trump's mail-in ballot rules incorrect in a sharp dissent.
story: Fox News contributor and constitutional law attorney Jonathan Turley discusses a federal judge’s decision to halt President Donald Trump’s executive order limiting mail-in voting on ‘America Reports.’

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas firmly dissented Monday as the Supreme Court denied a request by President Donald Trump's administration for relief from a universal injunction against its mail-in ballot rules.
The dissent, which Alito authored and Thomas joined, argued that the plaintiffs in the case were relying on claims that the court had previously identified as weak and unlikely to succeed.

"The Court incorrectly denies the Government’s application for a stay of a universal injunction that bars implementation of a final rule concerning election ballot mail," Alito wrote. "Some of the plaintiffs lack standing, while the remainder are pursuing a claim that this Court has recently called a ‘Hail Mary pass’ that ‘rarely succeeds.'"
SUPREME COURT REJECTS TRUMP BID TO REVIVE STRICT MAIL-BALLOT RULES BEFORE MIDTERMS
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito saying he is staying for another term drew praise from President Donald Trump. (Getty Images)
"The Government has made the showings necessary for a stay, so I respectfully dissent," he concluded.

The Court's Monday order went unsigned, but Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a concurrence that allowed room for a potential Trump victory down the line. He nevertheless argued that it is too close to Election Day to realistically implement the rules for the 2026 midterm elections.
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT REJECTS TRUMP BID TO ENFORCE MAIL BALLOT ORDER AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Supreme Court Associate Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas wait to leave the stage after the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/AFP via Getty Images)

"In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority," Kavanaugh wrote. "But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."
Kavanaugh's concurrence echoes Alito's dissent in acknowledging the expansive authority the USPS holds to regulate the collection, handling, transportation and delivery of mail.
USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE
The Trump rules would require federal ballot mail to be sent in envelopes bearing an election-mail logo, capable of being scanned by high-speed equipment and carrying a barcode unique to each voter.
The Supreme Court is seen, Jan. 13, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File)
State and local election officials would also be required to submit envelope designs to the Postal Service for review and upload basic voter information to an online USPS portal.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Under the USPS rule, mailings that failed to comply would not be accepted and would instead be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit.
Fox News' Stepheny Price and Shannon Bream contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Seven-figure blitz as GOP embraces push to compete with China in booming new tech space
summary: Alliance for a Better Future targets Bernie Sanders and AOC in new AI ads while praising three GOP lawmakers for balancing innovation and safeguards.
story: The Alliance for a Better Future is launching a multimillion-dollar ad campaign praising Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa for supporting AI safeguards and American innovation.

FIRST ON FOX: Three sitting Republican lawmakers, all facing midterm elections for U.S. Senate in less than two months, are paving the way for a pro-artificial intelligence push as Washington looks to balance regulation with American innovation despite the public's increasing skepticism over the emerging technology.

The conservative Alliance for a Better Future (ABF) is pouring millions into backing the campaigns of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, according to new ads shared exclusively with Fox News Digital ahead of their release.

The lawmakers, ABF says, mirror President Donald Trump's balanced stance on applying both safeguards and common sense to AI developments. When speaking on the topic in June, Trump said, "[AI] can be used for tremendous good, mostly good and some bad. And the bad we have to stop."
TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATES SCORE MAJOR BOOST FROM DEEP-POCKETED AI SUPER PAC IN UPCOMING PRIMARIES
President Donald Trump is seen during a meeting at Farmleigh House in Dublin, Ireland, on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP)

The advertisements come as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, over the weekend, warned the industry that his company helps lead to give safety measures more time to catch up with rapidly advancing AI capabilities. Just days earlier, an Anthropic researcher resigned while publicly raising concerns about the technology's risks. Anthropic is most known for its LLM AI Claude, one of the leading chatbots in the U.S.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, the father of ChatGPT, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis all expressed support for Amodei’s stance on slowing the pace of AI development.
Trump on Monday rejected the calls for implementing safeguards and restrictions on AI, arguing the technology needs a "STRONG AND SMART" president rather than added restraints.

The new advertisements, which will run throughout September, follow the ABF's previously unreported $1 million donation made to MAGA Inc. last week to promote candidates who share the group's values of pushing both innovation and security in emerging technologies like AI.

But the ads aren't limited to praising Republicans — they also take shots at the perceived risks ABF believes could result from allowing socialist lawmakers like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to lead policies dictating the direction of AI.
SANDERS PUSHES 'DEATH PENALTY' FOR CRUCIAL US INDUSTRY THAT COULD GIVE ADVANTAGE TO FOREIGN ADVERSARIES

Senator Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, speaks during a campaign event with Senator Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, not pictured, ahead of a primary election at IBEW Local 103 in the Dorchester neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts, on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"The same people who consistently fail you will write an AI rulebook for their benefit," the advertisement reads as images of Sanders, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., appear onscreen.

Security concerns have been top of mind for many Americans and AI experts as the United States races to stay ahead of China in technology developments, with worry that the rapidly increasing growth of AI poses national and cybersecurity threats.
"The only way we win the AI race against China is to build a technology that is trusted by the American people," ABF CEO Janet Kelly said in a statement to Fox News Digital on the new ad buys.

"We cannot cede this responsibility to Socialists like Bernie Sanders, who have a track record of destroying our economy and palling around with our enemies," she continued. "Conservatives like Susan Collins, Roger Marshall, and Ashley Hinson know the time is now to enact an agenda that ensures AI is built with American values."
Sanders’ office did not reply to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on being singled out in the campaign ads.
MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, departs the chamber at the Capitol in Washington, on July 24, 2025. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo)

Kelly, the former secretary of Health in Virginia, warned that China will "cheat and steal and lie" to beat the U.S. in the AI race in a policy event hosted by Breitbart news last week. She emphasized the need for America to be both diligent and urgent in developing this technology at a pace that puts the U.S. above foreign adversaries.
Collins, Marshall and Hinson have each backed policies that align with ABF’s goal to pursue AI development with protections that work to combat any emerging risks.

Hinson has argued that the U.S. must maintain its technological edge over Beijing while being thorough in analyzing AI's risks. Marshall acknowledged AI as a tool to assist, not replace American workers — also backing measures addressing its workforce and energy impacts.
Collins has supported federal investment in advanced computing while championing in Maine safeguards against deceptive AI-generated election content.
TRUMP-ENDORSED HINSON SECURES IOWA SENATE NOMINATION AS DEMOCRATS EYE GOP SEAT

ABF is a conservative AI policy organization that believes that as the technology continues to rapidly develop, American values should be prioritized — protecting children, the economy and national security.
The three GOP lawmakers are all Republican nominees for Senate seats in the upcoming midterm elections for their respective states.

Collins, Marshall and Hinson’s offices did not reply to Fox News Digital’s request to comment on the new advertisements and clarify their stances on AI.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: 'MAGA Act' could rip House seats from Dem states ahead of next presidential race
summary: The House GOP proposal would count only citizens for apportionment, with a CIS report saying noncitizens gave Democrat states a net 14 seats.
story: Virginia's removal of thousands of noncitizens from its voter rolls sparks renewed demands for election integrity.
FIRST ON FOX: A new House GOP proposal targeting the nation's congressional map could kneecap blue states and dramatically change their representation on Capitol Hill.
Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., is introducing legislation that would only count citizens when deciding how many House representatives each state gets, called the Make Apportionment Great Again (MAGA) Act.

It would be a fundamental change in congressional representation across the country, particularly hitting states where the most noncitizens live. The U.S. census has traditionally sought to count all people living within the country's borders, regardless of citizenship or even lawful status.
WHERE TRUMP, GOP VS DEMOCRATS REDISTRICTING BATTLE HEADS NEXT IN WAKE OF KEY COURT RULINGS

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul could see their states lose congressional seats under a new House GOP proposal. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images; Adam Gray/AP Photo/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

According to the U.S. census website, immigrants — both citizens and noncitizens — make up a fifth of the population in California, New Jersey, New York and Florida. Illegal immigrants living in sanctuary jurisdictions are also in theory counted by the census.

A 2024 report by the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS) said immigrants, both legal and illegal, resulted in a "net increase" of 14 seats in Democrat-leaning states. Republican states had 10 fewer seats than they otherwise would have, the report said.
MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES
The legislation would not require a new census after 2020, instead forcing states to rely on existing records to reapportion by sometime in 2027.

It would, however, add a new question to the 2030 census, asking people whether they are a U.S. citizen, U.S. national but not a citizen, an alien lawfully residing in the United States, or an alien unlawfully residing in the United States.
Close-up of someone holding a letter from the Census Bureau regarding the 2020 Census, in San Ramon, Calif., April 24, 2020. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
RNC LEGAL VICTORY CLEARS NORTH CAROLINA VOTER ROLL PURGE OF NONCITIZENS THROUGH JURY RESPONSES
But Clyde's bill could see a significant legal battle in the courts, even if passed.

The 14th Amendment to the Constitution states that House seats will be apportioned after "counting the whole number of persons in each State," not specifying citizenship status. It could invite challenges from pro-immigrant groups and left-wing organizations that have long been critical of GOP election efforts.
JACKSON ACCUSES THOMAS OF ECHOING INFAMOUSLY RACIST COURT DECISION IN BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CLASH
Clyde's bill comes after a video clip resurfaced in July that appears to show Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., claiming she needs more immigrants in her district "just for redistricting purposes."

The video, from a 2021 House Foreign Affairs Committee briefing, shows longtime Democrat Clarke suggesting that the local Haitian community in Brooklyn could "absorb a significant number of these migrants."

"When I hear my colleagues talk about, you know, the doors of the inn being closed, no room in the inn, I’m saying, you know, I need more people in my district, just for redistricting purposes and those members could clearly fit here," said Clarke.

Clarke's office did not respond to a request for comment at the time by Fox News Digital.

title: Trump’s data center push fractures Congress as local anger explodes: 'Grasping at straws'
summary: Democratic lawmakers push to restrict data centers over water use and electricity bills while Republicans highlight AI race benefits and local control.
story: Democratic lawmakers told Fox News Digital they want tighter regulations on data centers, while some Republicans voiced concerns over their impact on local communities. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Democratic lawmakers are calling for tighter restrictions on data centers, while Republicans say the facilities could boost the economy and keep the U.S. ahead in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.

President Donald Trump doubled down on data centers this week, rejecting calls to slow development after previously warning that communities blocking the facilities would "end up being backwards and poor."
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital last month that Arizona needs to slow the expansion of data centers until the state fully assesses its long-term impacts.

"We in Arizona need to pause the expansion of data centers in the state until we really figure out a plan on how we're going to preserve our water, how we are going to make sure that ratepayers aren't taking on the responsibility," Ansari said.
MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION
President Donald Trump arrives to speak during the first day of the Republican Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Bloomberg)
Ansari called President Trump's support for data centers "out of touch," saying it runs counter to what the "vast majority" of Americans want.
"If Donald Trump is such a big fan of data centers, then he should welcome them in his own backyard," she said.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., pointed to his proposed Data Center Bill of Rights, which would ban data centers within 2,500 feet of homes, schools, childcare facilities, hospitals and nursing homes and give communities greater authority over where they're built.
Khanna dismissed President Donald Trump's comments that communities opposing data centers would fall behind.
"Trump has failed to deliver for the forgotten American, so he's just grasping at straws," he said.
Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., said lawmakers must prioritize what's "fair" for local communities.
"The wealth has gone into the tech sector, and they are unregulated, unbridled and not very philanthropic," Jackson said.
WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

Protestors hold up "Stop data centers" signs, on the day of U.S. President Donald Trump's speech at the General Motors Proving Ground, in Milford, Michigan, U.S. July 27, 2026. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)
Higher electricity bills shouldn't fall on communities as data centers expand, according to Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.
"It baffles me that we are just not guaranteeing, for average ratepayers, low utility bills," she said. "These data centers could play a role in that."
Republican lawmakers were split on data centers, with some saying they can boost economies and others stressing local control.
Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., backed AI investment to compete with China but opposed building data centers in residential neighborhoods.
"We've got to stay ahead of China with AI, and data centers are a part of that," Mace said. "But you don't put them in somebody's backyard and that's the whole point."
Praising data centers, Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., said they can generate tax revenue, improve local infrastructure and support energy production.
CRACKDOWN ON CRITICAL TECH COULD OPEN AMERICANS TO A NEW NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT
The Austin Energy/Sand Hill Energy Center is seen in Austin, Texas, on July 28, 2026. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
"You should be fighting over them," McCormick said. "But, I mean, if you don't want one, that's up to you. I think you're missing out."
Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said decisions about data centers should be left to states and local communities.
"I believe in 10th Amendment rights, state rights," Norman said. "Let each community take ownership, and they'll make the right decisions."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
As several states raise concerns over electricity costs, water use and development, the debate highlights growing divisions over where data centers belong in local communities.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Voters have a blunt message for Trump about his idea to dole out $5,000 checks
summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend check proposal drew sharp reactions from voters, with some calling it a publicity stunt unlikely to pass Congress.
story: Fox News Digital spoke with voters about President Donald Trump's proposal to send Americans $5,000 checks if the GOP keeps control of Congress, revealing mixed concerns over the national debt. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Voters aren't convinced that President Donald Trump will make good on his new promise to send eligible Americans $5,000 dividend checks if Republicans maintain their majorities in the House and Senate this midterm cycle.

The proposal, which Trump unveiled during the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas last week, has ignited a national debate over whether the payments are financially feasible — and whether they'll ever become reality.

Asked what they thought of the proposal, and whether they believed it would ever become reality, most voters were skeptical, with several dismissing the idea as unrealistic while pointing to Congress, the nation's debt and previous promises they said never materialized.
A few were hopeful.
President Donald Trump's promise of a $5,000 dividend check has quickly become one of the most talked-about proposals of the midterm campaign. (The Dallas Morning News via GettyImages)
"Personally, I think it's just a publicity stunt and I don't think that it's ever gonna happen," a voter named William said when speaking with Fox News Digital.
"It'll need to go through Congress, and I don't think with the midterm elections... the possibility of that happening is just so far down the road."
TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN
As Fox News Digital previously reported, the dividend proposal would require congressional approval, and it's unclear where the money would come from to fund the program.
Another voter was clued into the dilemma and questioned whether the federal government, under it's 40.1 trillion in national debt, could afford the proposal.
"I don't think we have the money for that," said Daniel from Maryland. "And I think if we did, it should be going a couple different other places than that for sure."
Trump has repeatedly tied the proposal to the November elections, telling voters the payments would depend on Republicans retaining control of Congress. (AP Photo/Julio Cortez)
Liz from Alexandria, Virginia, was even more blunt, calling the idea "absolute nonsense."
"I don't believe a word that man ever says," she added in reference to Trump.
Another cited previous promises they believed had fallen short. "Last time I remember he promised a stimulus and a couple other things. None of that happened," the voter said.

The president argued the checks would be funded through tariff revenue — but with an estimated price tag of roughly $1.2 trillion, the total needed far exceeds the record customs duties the federal government has collected under Trump's tariff agenda.
TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE
The proposal comes as Republicans seek to convince voters that keeping the GOP in power would translate into more money in Americans' pockets. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Some voters said they welcomed the proposal, arguing that taxpayer dollars should go to hardworking Americans.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I think he's limiting it to American citizens and adults who work," one supporter told Fox News Digital.
"We've given a hell of a lot of money to people who don't deserve it," they added. "It's about time hardworking citizens of America get the money they deserve."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Raucous primary season reaches final act in deep-blue stronghold, kickstarting sprint to November
summary: Delaware's final 2026 primary caps a season when Donald Trump's endorsements dominated GOP races and progressive socialists ousted incumbents.
story: With 50 days until voters head to the polls, moderate Democrats struggle to find a place within the increasingly left-leaning Democratic Party. Guest panelists Jeremy Hunt and Michael LaRosa debate the impact of the change on 'The Faulkner Focus.'

Delaware voters head to the polls Tuesday for the final primary of the 2026 election cycle, capping a season marked by high-profile victories for progressives and socialists over Democratic establishment rivals and President Donald Trump’s continued immense influence in Republican contests, despite some notable setbacks.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons and state Attorney General Kathy Jennings each face primary opponents, and Democratic Rep. Sarah McBride is unopposed in her primary, as they tune up for the general election, when Republicans will try to break the Democrats' lock on Delaware's statewide offices.

Delaware's nominating contests close out a primary season that upended the Democratic Party, with left-wing and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-backed contenders winning and, in some cases, ousting longtime incumbents.

A year after socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rocked the political world with a Democratic primary victory en route to winning the general election in the nation's most populist city, the far-left struck again in June.
CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Congressional candidate Claire Valdez, Congressional candidate Brad Lander, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier raise their hands during a Get Out the Vote rally at King's Theater on June 18, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

A slew of incumbents and establishment candidates were defeated by left-wing rivals, including DSA members Melat Kiros topping 15-term incumbent Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York ousting five-term Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York.

Those wins were followed on an even larger scale in August, with triumphs in crucial statewide Senate primaries by Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and state Rep. Angie Nixon in Florida.

While there were notable setbacks for the left, including frontrunner Francesca Hong's August defeat in battleground Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, the left vastly increased its clout in the political fight for the party's ideological future. And many of the winning candidates ran on platforms calling for abolishing ICE, cutting military aid to Israel and pushing for a single-payer "Medicare for All" health system.

"It is undeniable that progressives have built a coalition and have a message that can serve to buoy a candidate when they are an acceptable alternative to the status quo," longtime Democratic strategist Joe Caiazzo, a veteran of progressive champion Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, told Fox News Digital.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in battleground Michigan, takes questions from reporters following a town hall event in Waterford, Michigan, on Sept. 3, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Getty Images)
Caiazzo added, "What's incumbent upon progressives if they want to continue to be successful is to put forward candidates who are serious, credible and are accessible to the public."
In Republican nominating battles, Trump took to social media late last month to tout, "My Endorsements are stronger than ever....There has never been anything close!"
The numbers back up the president's assertion that despite some setbacks, he remains the ultimate kingmaker in GOP nomination showdowns.

According to a Fox News Trump Primary Endorsement Tracker, the president batted a thousand in Senate GOP primaries this cycle and enjoyed a near-perfect record in House Republican nomination showdowns.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

U.S. President Donald Trump points as he arrives to speak during a campaign rally for U.S. Sen. Darline Graham at Myrtle Beach Convention Center in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Aug. 21, 2026. (SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images)

Trump has dramatically reshaped the GOP since his first White House victory a decade ago, with the populist MAGA and America First wings gaining prominence over more traditional fiscal and social conservatives. And the president's grip over party politics remains extremely firm.

But he has had some setbacks, with five of his gubernatorial picks in Republican primaries this year going down to defeat. That list includes Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, Rep. Randy Feenstra of Iowa, Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder and Minnesota businessman and "My Pillow" founder and former CEO Mike Lindell.

"The Republican Party is Trump’s party, and there’s no question that an endorsement from the president provides a tremendous boost in a Republican primary. But it doesn’t necessarily mean the candidate’s going to win," veteran GOP strategist and communicator Ryan Williams told Fox News Digital.

Williams said that "the president still has a firm grip on the party, even in places where a candidate he backed loses a nomination." But he noted that "if there are underlying issues with a candidacy, those can pose problems that even an endorsement can’t overcome."
After a primary season that kicked off on March 3 in Texas, North Carolina, Arkansas and Delaware bring the calendar to a close.
Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware is running this year for a third full term in the U.S. Senate.

Coons, who is running for a third full term in the Senate, is facing longshot primary challenges from University of Delaware history professor Jeff Appelhans, naval architect Mary Louve and former business executive Eric Hansen, a Republican turned Democrat.
Former state Sen. Michael Katz and U.S. Army Reserves Col. John Shulli are competing for the Republican nomination.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Rep. Sarah McBride is unopposed in the Democratic primary, as she seeks a second term as Delaware's statewide House member. Republicans Joseph Arminio, Earl Cooper and John Whalen are battling for the GOP nomination.

State Attorney General Kathy Jennings faces challenges for the Democratic nomination from attorney Dwayne Bensing and domestic violence victims advocate Patty Rickman. David Graham is unopposed for the GOP nomination.
The Associated Press contributed to this report
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Surrogate who refused abortion asks SCOTUS to intervene as baby could be moved out of Texas
summary: Surrogate McKenna West asked the Supreme Court for an emergency administrative stay, fearing the newborn could be moved from Texas to California.
story: Former federal prosecutor Andrew Cherkasky discusses a surrogate’s legal battle with the biological parents over a baby with a rare heart condition on ‘Fox Report.’

The surrogate who refused an abortion sought by the biological parents has filed an updated brief with the U.S. Supreme Court following an emergency application she filed with the court last week, arguing the case is moving more quickly than expected.

McKenna West, an Alaska resident, and a California couple referred to as the commissioning parties, have been involved in a legal battle after she refused their request to terminate the pregnancy after a diagnosis of a serious heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS).

Represented by attorneys from Alliance Defending Freedom and First & Fourteenth PLLC, West asked Justice Elena Kagan, who handles emergency matters from the Ninth Circuit, for an administrative stay and a stay pending a possible petition for certiorari.
SURROGATE, CALIFORNIA COUPLE CLASH IN COURT AS NEWBORN FIGHTS FOR LIFE AFTER HEART SURGERY
Surrogate mother McKenna West, who fled to Texas after her baby's birth parents asked her to abort the child. (Live Action)

Her application argues that the California courts violated federal due process by treating her jurisdictional defense as consent. It also argues that without a stay, the baby could be moved to California for hospice care while West remains unable to participate in decisions about the child's medical treatment.
But on Monday, the surrogate and her team expressed fears that the baby may be moved out of Texas earlier than she had expected.
She is asking the high court for an administrative stay 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday.
SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION
On Monday, the surrogate and her team expressed fears that the baby may be moved out of Texas earlier than she had expected. (LM Otero/AP Photo)
This comes after a California court judgment that declared the commissioning parents the child's legal parents and denied West's custody claims.
The commissioning parents have argued in court that California has jurisdiction under the surrogacy agreement and that they are the child's legal parents.

West had refused the commissioning parents' request for an abortion and traveled to Texas, which has abortion restrictions, to give birth, saying she did so to ensure access to specialized medical care.

She asked for parentage and protective orders in Alaska and Texas, but the commissioning parents filed a parentage action in the Los Angeles Superior Court, according to Fox 4. West entered a special appearance to contest personal jurisdiction and object to the forum, citing a forum-selection clause that required litigation to be held in Alaska.
The surrogate is asking the high court for an administrative stay by 1 p.m. on Tuesday. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But the California trial court ruled that West’s jurisdictional arguments and attached exhibits constituted a general appearance, meaning she had consented to the court’s jurisdiction, the outlet reported. The court then entered an ex parte judgment of parentage in favor of the commissioning parents.

After the baby was born in Texas on Aug. 12, a Texas court recognized the California ruling naming the commissioning couple as his legal parents and dismissed West from the case with prejudice, meaning she could not refile the same claim in that proceeding.

title: ‘Trojan horses’ in America: Congress probes influence networks tied to China, Iran and Cuba
summary: Lawmakers will examine alleged foreign malign influence operations tied to China, Iran and Cuba after Fox News Digital traced pro-communist network operating inside the U.S.
story: D.C. CodePink organizer Olivia DiNucci shouted and unfurled a ‘SANCTIONS KILL IN CUBA’ during a panel discussion at the Institute of World Politics on Sept. 8, 2026, in Washington, D.C., before security removed her. (Credit: CodePink via Storyful)

Last Tuesday, at the corner of Church Street and 16th Street NW, blocks from the White House, Christine Balling, a former advisor to U.S. Special Operations Command South, led a panel discussion on the national security threat that communist-run Cuba poses to the U.S.

Suddenly, a fresh-faced former college basketball star, Olivia DiNucci, stood up to steal the stage at the Institute of World Politics, yelling as she clutched a hand-painted banner: "SANCTIONS KILL IN CUBA."

"There is global solidarity with Gaza and Cuba and ICE here," DiNucci shouted breathlessly, as security officials grabbed her banner and pushed her out a side door as she kept yelling, "because the liberation of our people is rooted in our neighbors!"
In small print, the banner had DiNucci's organizational and ideological affiliation: "CODEPINK."

DiNucci is a D.C.-based political organizer with CodePink, a left-wing political agitation group, spending her days and evenings as a professional protester and a regular gadfly, disrupting dinners, hearings and conferences as a sidekick to CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin. Their group supports the Communist Party of Cuba and has led caravans to the island nation, as Treasury Department officials investigate whether they violated any laws barring Americans from doing business with the communist regime.

For Balling and her co-panelist, Michael Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation and a Cuban American firmly opposed to the communist government of Cuba, DiNucci's political theater wasn't the benign act of an "anti-war" group, as CodePink describes itself.
"CodePink – and other organizations like it – essentially act like Trojan horses. They burst in onto the scene, and they're meant to disrupt and destroy from within," Balling told Fox News Digital.

"They're really interested in dividing America and, in doing so, weakening it," she continued, "and increasing the friction between Americans by convincing some Americans that the American idea, the American dream, the freedoms we enjoy, all that sort of thing, that they are lies and they're not worth fighting for, and that our enemies are our victims."
POWER COUPLE OF CHAOS: HOW A TYCOON AND ACTIVIST BUILT A 'REVOLUTIONARY BASE' AT THE HOUSE OF SINGHAM
Medea Benjamin (right) and Olivia DiNucci (center) of CodePink protest against the U.S. war in Iran. (Fox News Digital)

The confrontation comes as House lawmakers convene a hearing on Tuesday, titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America," to examine a broad question: how do American activists, nonprofit organizations, media operations and social media influencers, like Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, advance the interests of adversarial nations, including China, Iran and Cuba, inside the United States?
Piker joined CodePink's delegation to Cuba earlier this year, posing for a photo in Havana with CodePink cofounder, Jodie Evans, both of them also drawing Treasury Department scrutiny.

"Adversarial nations like China, Russia, and Cuba conduct malign influence operations here in the United States by utilizing social media influencers such as Hasan Piker as proxies to promote communism and push their false propaganda," Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, told Fox News Digital.
"My goal is to raise the curtain to expose these operations and stop them from undermining our national security, capitalism and the American Dream," Huizenga said.
HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA

Democratic Socialists of America member Hasan Piker and CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans of CodePink meet in Cuba, as part of "United Front" to support the communist regime. (NO ACCESS EDGE/NNS/FNS/OUTKICK) (CodePink via Storyful)

The hearing will bring together several strands of alleged foreign influence that Fox News Digital has documented over the past year through investigations into money, political organizing, overseas travel, media operations and relationships between American activists and foreign entities and interests. Most of the groups fall into the "red-green alliance" of socialist and communist groups, symbolized by the color red, working closely with Islamist groups, such as the anti-Israel organization Students for Justice in Palestine, reflected by the color green, a symbol of Islam.

The largest financial network examined in Fox News Digital's reporting centers on Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon who lives in Shanghai, late last year standing on a stage at the Golden Tulip Hotel during a conference on the "Global South," delivering a speech supporting the Chinese Communist Party, China's leader, Xi Jinping and China's "new world order."
RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS

A five-part Fox News Digital investigation published earlier this year examined 223 transactions totaling $591 million across five continents between 2017 and 2025, tracing the flow of money through multiple layers of organizations and into a transnational network estimated at approximately 2,000 organizations.

In 2017, Singham married Evans, the CodePink co-founder, in a ceremony in Jamaica attended by Benjamin and other pro-communist leaders. The Fox News Digital analysis documented $278 million flowing from Singham into six core nonprofit organizations that promulgate anti-America, pro-China propaganda, beginning in 2017: BreakThrough BT Media Inc., CodePink Women for Peace, Justice and Education Fund Inc., People's Forum Inc., People's Support Foundation Ltd. and Tricontinental Ltd.
The organizations and their executives have denied any wrongdoing and allege they are the target of anti-communist "witch hunts." Singham hasn't responded to repeated requests for comment.
CUBA BUILT COVERT NETWORK INSIDE AMERICA THROUGH SPIES, ACTIVISTS AND UNIVERSITIES, STATE DEPT ALLEGES

On Feb. 14, 2018, Jodie Evans, co-founder founder of CodePink, and Neville Roy Singham, founder of Thoughtworks, attend V20: The Red Party, a 20th anniversary celebration of V-Day and The Vagina Monologues, featuring a performance by playwright Eve Ensler and an after-party at Carnegie Hall in New York City. (Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images)

Huizenga and the hearing's witnesses say Congress must examine whether adversarial governments are influencing American political discourse through domestic messengers while keeping the foreign power itself at arm's length.
Fox News Digital's reporting followed the money to the six nonprofits:
$167.5 million to People's Support Foundation Ltd., a nonprofit based in Chicago, with CodePink's Evans on the board, funneling money to overseas projects;
$68.7 million to Justice and Education Fund Inc., a New York City-based nonprofit that funnels grants to far-left causes domestically and overseas;
$22.44 million to the People's Forum, a hub for pro-communist organizing in New York City;
$16.76 million to Tricontinental Ltd., a Massachusetts-based think tank led by a friend of Singham's, Vijay Prashad, who led a session on the future of Marxism at Singham's wedding to Evans.
$1.33 million to CodePink, a California-based far-left, pro-Cuba, pro-China group that has supported the Islamic Republic of Iran and anti-Israel campaigns;

$1.098 million to BreakThrough BT Media, a New York-based propaganda arm of the network that runs BreakThrough News, a media outfit that is often the first to broadcast images and videos of anti-America protests.

That was only the first layer. The six nonprofits that directly received Singham money subsequently distributed approximately $163 million to 52 organizations — including themselves — and five geographic regions identified in financial records.

Eleven groups at another layer distributed approximately $150 million into four nonprofits and five geographic regions, including $23 million directed to Sub-Saharan Africa, according to the Fox News Digital analysis.

The financial architecture has been accompanied by political organizing, media operations and ideological activity that includes the fresh example of political theater that CodePink unleashed at this week's disruption at the Institute of World Politics' panel on Cuba.
Balling, the former advisor to U.S. Special Operations Southern Command, used the opportunity to illustrate exactly the point that the Heritage Foundation's Gonzalez and she were arguing.
"Their method of operation," she said, "is to disrupt, of course, to get the soundbites on Twitter or Instagram or what have you, but they are not ever interested in a respectful dialogue."

"What was extraordinary is I was actually about to talk about CodePink and the Democratic Socialists of America, the DSA, as both being members of the largest pro-Cuban regime organization in the United States, called the National Network on Cuba," said Balling.

WASHINGTON DC, UNITED STATES - MARCH 6: United States Rep. Bill Huizenga speaks during a hearing before the House Financial Services Committee at the Rayburn House Office Building in Washington, D.C., on March 6, 2024. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"And so the fact that she stood up and tried to disrupt the event was just a wonderful example for the audience," of the antics of CodePink. "They are actually really a mouthpiece for anti-American causes, which happen to be very pro-Chinese Communist Party causes and...the Castro regime."

On cue, at 6:42 p.m., less than an hour after the event had ended at about 6 p.m., CodePink posted a carefully curated and captioned 1-minute-35-second video of the DiNucci outburst on X. The same video went up on CodePink's official YouTube channel.
Balling said CodePink's messaging promoted "the interests of, frankly, our enemies, the Chinese Communist Party and then the Cuban regime."

On June 4, 2024, CodePink's Medea Benjamin interrupts a Capitol Hill news conference in Washington, D.C., organized to commemorate the anniversary of the 1989 Tiananmen Square Massacre and to discuss the "ongoing struggle for human rights and democracy in China." Her sign says, "China is not our enemy." (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images))
"Their method of operation," she said, "is to disrupt, of course, to get the soundbites on Twitter or Instagram or what have you, but they are not ever interested in a respectful dialogue."
Sure enough, CodePink posted the video on its official Instagram account, tagging DiNucci.
"Frankly, had she been willing to stop screaming," said Balling, Gonzalez and she "would have actually been thrilled to have a debate with her, but that's not their way of operating."
By the end of the night, the disruption had also become a press release on CodePink's website, listing DiNucci herself as the "media contact" and offering journalists "unbranded video footage."

title: House Dems face Trump tariff dilemma as major Russia sanctions bill heads to floor
summary: The Lindsey Graham sanctions bill forces House Democrats to weigh Ukraine support against expanding Trump tariff authority they've long opposed.
story: A Senate-passed Russia sanctions bill faces resistance in the House as Democrats raise concerns about granting President Trump expanded tariff authority, while supporters argue tougher economic pressure could help force Moscow toward negotiations.

House Democrats will soon have to grapple with a decision over whether to give President Donald Trump more tariff authority or potentially block Congress from cracking down on Vladimir Putin's bloody war in Ukraine.
The House Rules Committee has teed up votes on several bills this week, including the Senate's legislation aimed at sanctioning Russia and Iran.
That bill was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., a massive supporter of Ukraine who died unexpectedly at the age of 71 in July.

And while the majority of Democrats support action to help Ukraine against Russia's invasion, they'll also be forced to reckon with the legislation's language giving Trump additional authority to punish Russia and its allies with significant tariffs.
LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION TO PUNISH PUTIN CLEARS SENATE AFTER YEARLONG FIGHT

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol building on March 27, 2026 in Washington, D.C. President of the United States Donald J. Trump during the 2026 Easter Egg Roll at the White House, Washington, D.C., on April 6, 2026. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images; Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Democrats have long been critical of Trump's unchecked use of tariffs against U.S. allies like Canada and Mexico, which have also been subject to a slew of court battles.
TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED
It's part of why senior House Democrats said earlier this year that they would oppose the bill.

"House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good. This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., Ranking Member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., Ranking Member of the House Committee on Ways and Means, and Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said in a statement.
SEN RAND PAUL: DC'S RUSSIA SANCTIONS BILL WON'T STOP PUTIN — BUT IT WILL HURT YOU

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., did not give up his position on the bill during a Monday press conference, telling reporters, "We're going to continue to stand by the Ukrainian people and find a path forward to get a sanctions bill done while addressing the very real concerns that [Democrats] have raised about giving Donald Trump authority that the Supreme Court recently made clear he does not currently have, and should not have, because it belongs to the Congress pursuant to the Constitution."
The bill would direct the president to hike up to 500% tariffs on Russia and up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy.
MIKE PENCE: CONGRESS MUST FINISH LINDSEY GRAHAM’S FIGHT AGAINST PUTIN
Trump would also be directed to impose significant sanctions on Russian officials and others responsible for continuing the war on Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, meets with Sen. Lindsey Graham in Kyiv, Ukraine, on March 18, 2024. (Ukrainian Presidency/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The bill advanced through the House Rules Committee on Monday night, setting up a House-wide procedural hurdle called a "rule vote" on Tuesday afternoon.
If passed, the full House will vote on the sanctions bill on Wednesday afternoon, according to a preliminary legislative schedule obtained by Fox News Digital.
And with an increasingly vocal isolationist wing permeating the House GOP Conference, at least some Democrats will be needed to help the bill pass.

The package, pushed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Graham, was in purgatory for nearly two years as the lawmakers and administration went back and forth to find a compromise that Trump and Congress could stomach.

Blumenthal defended the tariff language in the bill to Fox News Digital, "If Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously."
And Senate Democrats largely voted in favor of giving Trump limited tariff authority in exchange for the bone-crushing sanctions against Russia, despite raging against duties for years.

In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow on September 5, 2026. (Gavriil GRIGOROV / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Though some raised concerns, like Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., most Democratic caucus members gave a thumbs-up to the tariff power.
EXCLUSIVE: PENCE PUSHES TO RENAME BILL FOR LINDSEY GRAHAM, RECALLS FINAL TALK: 'BRING PUTIN TO THE TABLE'

That all came after Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., received guarantees from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the tariffs baked into the sanctions package would just be limited to the top five energy trading partners with the Kremlin.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to revive strict mail-ballot rules before midterms
summary: A lower court's nationwide block on U.S. Postal Service mail-in ballot rules remains after the Supreme Court ruled against the Trump administration.
story: Jason Snead accused Democratic-led states of resisting new USPS mail-ballot standards, while attorney Gregory Teufel argued the federal court overstepped its authority in blocking their implementation.

The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s emergency bid to enforce new U.S. Postal Service (USPS) restrictions on mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, leaving a lower court’s nationwide block in place.

In a brief order, the court said the government was "unlikely to succeed on the merits" for purposes of obtaining emergency relief and had not shown that the legal and practical considerations warranted a stay.
The rules would require federal ballot mail to be sent in envelopes bearing an election-mail logo, capable of being scanned by high-speed equipment and carrying a barcode unique to each voter.
State and local election officials would also be required to submit envelope designs to the Postal Service for review and upload basic voter information to an online USPS portal.
USPS PUBLISHES RULE TO BLOCK MAIL-IN BALLOTS FROM STATES THAT DON'T PROVIDE VOTER LISTS
A large box of pre-assembled mail-in ballots at the Wake County Board of Elections on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Raleigh, N.C. (Matt Ramey/AP Photo)
Under the USPS rule, mailings that failed to comply would not be accepted and would instead be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
A federal judge previously blocked the USPS from implementing the rules, including the online portal that could be used to track millions of mail ballots.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed with the Supreme Court’s decision but indicated the USPS may ultimately have the authority to impose the requirements.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS
Oregon residents drop off their ballots near the Multnomah County Elections building in Portland, Oregon, on Nov. 3, 2020. (Ankur Dholakia/AFP via Getty Images)

"In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority," Kavanaugh wrote.

However, he said attempting to apply the rules during the 2026 elections would be "arbitrary and capricious" under the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have enough time to reasonably implement them.
JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER

Supreme Court Associate Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas wait to leave the stage after the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/AFP via Getty Images)
Justice Samuel Alito dissented from the decision, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas.
Alito argued that some of the plaintiffs lacked legal standing and that the remaining challengers were pursuing what the court has previously called a "Hail Mary pass" that "rarely succeeds."
ALABAMA AG MARSHALL FIRES BACK AT USPS MAIL-BALLOT ORDER CRITICS: ‘THIS IS ABOUT SECURING ELECTIONS’
"The Government has made the showings necessary for a stay, so I respectfully dissent," Alito wrote.

Alito said the USPS has broad authority to regulate the collection, handling, transportation and delivery of mail. He also argued that the government would suffer irreparable harm because any reversal of the lower court’s injunction would come too late for the midterms.
New York Attorney General Letitia James, whose office helped lead the legal challenge, celebrated the decision as a victory for voters.

"Today, the Supreme Court protected one of our most fundamental, inalienable rights – the right to make your voice heard at the ballot box," James said. "This last-minute change could have thrown our elections into chaos, and I am truly relieved the Court granted this reprieve."

"Voters should never have to wonder whether a ballot they legally cast will be counted because the federal government suddenly changed the rules," she added. "We will keep fighting to make sure every eligible ballot is counted come November."
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., also praised the ruling, calling it "one of the most important cases to protect voting rights before the Supreme Court."
"Trump’s plan to make it harder to vote was obviously unconstitutional," Schumer said. "The Supreme Court had no choice but to make the right decision."
"The President’s attempt to screw around with vote by mail was obscene," he added. "Finally, his scheme is dead. Trump: you lost another one."
FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS
President Donald Trump directed the USPS earlier this year to develop new standards for handling election mail. The agency finalized the requirements in late August.
The administration and the USPS then asked the Supreme Court to intervene after a federal judge converted a temporary restraining order into a nationwide preliminary injunction.

The decision leaves the preliminary injunction in place, preventing the USPS from enforcing the new requirements for the 2026 elections while the litigation continues.

title: Mamdani blasts feds for waging 'campaign of violence and terror' against NYC's immigrants
summary: Zohran Mamdani condemned ICE raids and federal immigration policies as New York City joined other sanctuary jurisdictions in a lawsuit.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke out against the Trump administration's new public charge rule, which is set to expand the list of public benefits that can count against green card or visa applicants.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday blasted the federal government for waging a "campaign of violence and terror" against the immigrant communities he described as the backbone of the city.

He made the statements during an announcement that he and five other sanctuary jurisdictions are suing the Trump administration over a new rule expanding how immigration officials determine whether applicants are likely to become a public charge.
"The federal government has waged a campaign of violence and terror," Mamdani said.

"ICE has broken into our neighbors' homes, work sites and schools. And it has targeted those who have come to our country in search of refuge and in search of opportunity. These actions are an assault on our civic fabric, on our shared values. And no matter how much destruction they have already caused, it continues."
MAMDANI, LETITIA JAMES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN FROM REFUSING IMMIGRANTS OVER WELFARE STATUS

FILE — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a news conference in Queens on Nov. 5, 2025. Mamdani said ICE has targeted immigrant homes, workplaces and schools across the city. (Heather Khalifa/AP Photo)
Mamdani further credited immigrants from around the world with helping build and sustain New York City, including by contributing to its infrastructure and public services.

"Immigrants from every country, from every continent, who speak every language and worship in every conceivable way, drive our buses and our trains, teach our children how to read, and tend to us when we are sick," Mamdani said.
"Immigrants fought for the 8-hour workday for fair pay and workplace protections that deliver dignity into the lives of so many," he added.
AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

FILE — An ICE agent monitors asylum seekers in New York City on June 6, 2023. Mamdani accused federal immigration officials of targeting people seeking refuge and opportunity in the U.S. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images)

The city will lead a coalition of five other sanctuary jurisdictions, including Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, Santa Clara County and King County, in challenging the Trump administration’s stricter version of the public charge rule, which is set to take effect Friday.

The changes, issued in July by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), will expand officers’ discretion to weigh noncash benefits, such as Medicaid, SNAP and housing vouchers, when determining whether an immigrant is likely to become a public charge.

Under the previous guidelines, established in 2022 under the Biden administration, officers’ discretion was narrowed to consider only whether applicants were likely to become "primarily dependent" on government assistance based on cash benefits, such as Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).
In response to New York City filing the lawsuits, the White House on Monday blasted Democrats for seeking to provide illegal aliens with support at the expense of American taxpayers.

"Extreme Democrats are once again fighting to give benefits to illegal aliens at the expense of American taxpayers. Immigrants must be able to support themselves and not depend on hard-working American taxpayers. President Trump and this administration will always put American citizens first," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.
Mamdani described the changes as a "gross illegality" that will cause "irreparable damage."

"Make no mistake, this is an undisguised effort to strip New Yorkers of the services they rely on, the public benefits they are entitled to. Families, including those with children who are U.S. citizens, have already begun to forego essential services like SNAP, Medicaid, and affordable housing out of the fear that if they use these programs, immigration officers could use it as justification to deny them a future in our country," he said.

FILE — Protesters take over the lobby of a Manhattan hotel during an anti-ICE demonstration. New York City is leading a legal challenge with Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, Santa Clara County and King County over changes to the public charge rule. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler previously said the move is intended to safeguard the financial well-being of American taxpayers.

"The Trump administration is upholding the rule of law and protecting American taxpayers from subsidizing aliens who may become dependent on public benefits. USCIS is committed to safeguarding the safety, security, and financial well-being of Americans," Kahler said in a statement.
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

title: House unanimously votes to eliminate 1-cent coin permanently
summary: The Common Cents Act passed the House to officially end penny minting and establish cash rounding to the nearest nickel for cash transactions.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's upcoming test vote on landmark cryptocurrency legislation. He breaks down the political battle over the bill, including President Donald Trump's support for the crypto industry and opposition from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Adam Schiff, D-Calif.
Americans may soon no longer be able to offer a penny for their thoughts — because the 1-cent coin will be relegated to the ash heap of history.
The House of Representatives voted to send the smallest piece of U.S. currency the way of the dodo on Monday, passing the bipartisan Common Cents Act in a unanimous vote.

In addition to blocking the Treasury from minting any more pennies save for collector coins, the bill would also set up a framework for cash transactions to be rounded to the nearest 5 cents, in order to eliminate the need for pennies altogether.
AMERICANS SAY TIPPING PRACTICES 'HAVE BECOME RIDICULOUS' AS DIGITAL PROMPTS PUSH HIGHER GRATUITIES

Signage at the memorial site of the "funeral for the penny," months after U.S. President Donald Trump's administration ordered the Treasury Department to halt production of the coins, at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., U.S., December 20, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)
An exception would be provided for cash wages, which must be rounded upwards if the total is not divisible by 5 cents.
Existing pennies will still remain legal tender.
TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies in November 2025 after 232 years of circulation. But an act of Congress, if signed into law by President Donald Trump, would ensure a future administration does not reverse course.
Chairwoman Lisa McClain Hosts "A Warning to America: Stories from Survivors of Communism" Roundtable. (Courtesy of House Republican Conference)

The cost of minting pennies has risen dramatically in recent years, costing more than three times their value to produce as of 2025. The Treasury estimated an immediate annual savings of $56 million in a press release explaining the decision.
The bill was led by House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

It builds on a past bill McClain led in the House that also passed the Senate directing the federal government to stop minting the penny, but that legislation did not include language on rounding out cash payments.
An additional provision would allow the U.S. Mint to produce nickels from cheaper material than they currently are made with.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Congress would also monitor any disruptions the new rule causes to Americans by directing the Treasury to examine its effect on low-income people, older consumers, debanked people, among other groups.

title: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed says leaders must address ‘unpaid debts’ to Black communities
summary: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities.
story: A 'Fox News Sunday' panel discuss the crucial battleground Senate races in Michigan and Texas.

Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Saturday that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities, arguing that leaders have a responsibility to "understand" and "address" them.

El-Sayed — who is facing Republican nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races — made the remarks while speaking at a meeting with women faith leaders hosted by the Woman Difference Collaborative in Detroit, according to a video shared by C-SPAN.

"When it comes to black communities in Michigan — when it comes to black communities in America — there are unpaid debts that have long since come due that we are unwilling to acknowledge, let alone pay down," El-Sayed said.  "And I understand that we need leaders who are going to understand those debts and address them."
ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
El-Sayed made the remarks while responding to a question about how he plans to energize Democratic voters who did not support him in the primary.
He said his approach is to keep showing up, engaging with voters and emphasizing his record.

"But the question for me is, within my power have I done my best?" El-Sayed said. "And I will challenge people to look at my history and say, ‘Yeah, that man hasn’t done everything he could around the problems he says he cares about.'"
ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative, is pictured here. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
During his response, El-Sayed highlighted his work on infant and maternal mortality, asthma and lead exposure.
He also called for expanding access to capital for small businesses and increasing investment in housing and schools.
El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018 before launching his Senate campaign.
EL-SAYED’S LIBERAL AGENDA CLASHES WITH MUSLIM VOTERS WHO BACK HIM ANYWAY: ‘MALE VERSION’ OF ILHAN OMAR
El-Sayed and Rogers are competing in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The Detroit event also featured discussion of El-Sayed's public health record, U.S. aid to Israel, his endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, campaign attack ads from Rogers and criminal justice issues, according to C-SPAN.

El-Sayed's campaign could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.
